mainTopic: The dawn announcement in the מקדש, learning from אברהם's conduct, and the nature of light on cloudy days
overview: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא that gives five versions of the dawn announcement that signaled the time to slaughter the morning תמיד. It explains that רבי יהודה בן בתירא's 'people have gone out' means going out to hire workers. רב ספרא then says אברהם prayed מנחה as soon as the walls darkened. רבא first shows that a תנא learned from אברהם (זריזין מקדימין למצוות), and then explains that רב יוסף's real difficulty was the ערב פסח משנה that places the תמיד at six and a half hours. The גמרא gives three answers: the walls of the מקדש darkened late, or אברהם had special knowledge from astronomy, or from sitting in ישיבה. That last answer leads into a list of proofs that our ancestors always had a ישיבה, and to רב's teaching that אברהם kept the whole Torah, even עירובי תבשילין. Back in the משנה, the גמרא works out who said 'הן' in the dawn check, and explains that moonlight was mistaken for sunrise because it was a cloudy day. The amud ends with רב פפא's and רב נחמן's teachings about sunlight on cloudy days.

steps.title: Five versions of the dawn announcement
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records five opinions about the exact words the lookout used to announce dawn in the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי ישמעאל says the call was 'The light flashed.' רבי עקיבא says it was 'The light has risen.' נחומא בן אפקשיון says it was 'There is light even in חברון.' מתיא בן שמואל says the priest in charge of the lotteries announced: 'The whole eastern sky is lit up, all the way to חברון.' רבי יהודה בן בתירא says the call was: 'The whole eastern sky is lit up, all the way to חברון, and all the people have gone out, each one to his work.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה said someone would announce 'ברקאי' when dawn arrived. Here the גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists different versions of what exactly was said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each version describes a slightly brighter stage of dawn, moving from a quick flash of light, to light that has really risen, to light that reaches as far as חברון. רבי יהודה בן בתירא's version goes furthest, because it adds that people are already heading out to work. That extra detail sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: Morning light / the first glow of dawn
The priest appointed over the lotteries
The whole face of the east is lit up
חברון, a city to the south. Its light was a sign of real dawn

steps.confusionAlert: All five opinions describe the same announcement, the one that signaled it was time to slaughter the morning תמיד. Do not read them as separate announcements. They differ in its wording and in how much morning light it describes.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Yishmael says: "The light flashed."
Rabbi Akiva says: "The light has risen."
Nachuma ben Apakshiyon says:
"There is light even in Hebron."
Matya ben Shmuel (says):
The one appointed over the lotteries says:
"The whole eastern sky is lit, up to the area in Hebron."
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says:
"The whole eastern sky is lit, up to Hebron,

phrases.aramaic: וְיָצְאוּ כׇּל הָעָם אִישׁ אִישׁ לִמְלַאכְתּוֹ״.
phrases.english: and all the people have gone out, each man to his work."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's single word 'ברקאי' into a full list of opinions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are five versions of the dawn announcement, each describing a progressively brighter stage of morning light.

steps.title: If people went to work, isn't it already too late?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה בן בתירא: if people are already going to work, it must be well past dawn.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, it has gotten much lighter!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רבי יהודה בן בתירא's version. People do not go to work at the first light of dawn. They go when it is already bright.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The announcement is supposed to mark the very start of dawn, the earliest time to slaughter the תמיד. If it says people have already gone to work, it seems to describe a much later time. That would not fit the purpose of the call.

phrases.english: If so,
it has become very light already?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the last opinion in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה בן בתירא's wording 'all the people have gone out to their work'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Going to work happens in full daylight, but the announcement must mark the very beginning of dawn.

steps.title: They went out to hire workers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'going out' means the employers went out early to hire workers, not that the workers started working.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are talking about going out to hire workers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The people who 'went out' were field owners heading out at dawn to hire laborers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hiring is done very early, so that the work itself can begin once it is fully light. The phrase in רבי יהודה בן בתירא's version therefore still describes the start of dawn, and his version fits the purpose of the announcement.

keyTerms.meaning: We are saying / this is what we mean

phrases.english: We are speaking of going out to hire workers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the case (what 'going out' means)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Going out 'to work' means actually beginning labor, which happens in full daylight.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means going out to hire workers, which happens right at dawn.
steps.whatToRemember: All five versions describe dawn. Even 'people going out' refers to the early hiring of workers, not to the work itself.

steps.title: אברהם prayed מנחה as soon as the walls darkened
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא says that אברהם's afternoon prayer began as soon as shadows appeared on the walls.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: אברהם's prayer was from when the walls begin to darken.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new point about the time for מנחה. רב ספרא says אברהם prayed it as soon as the sun passed midday and the walls started to fall into shade.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the sun moves past the middle of the sky, shadows begin to fall on walls, and that marks the start of the afternoon. רב ספרא is using אברהם's conduct as a guide for when the time of מנחה begins. That is exactly what the next step questions.

keyTerms.meaning: From when the walls turn dark (with shade)

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
The prayer of Abraham
is from when the walls become dark.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement about the time of מנחה, following the earlier discussion of times of day in the מקדש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The time for מנחה begins when the sun passes midday and shadows appear on the walls, as shown by אברהם's practice.

steps.title: Can we learn הלכה from אברהם?
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף objects that we should not derive הלכה from אברהם's personal conduct.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Should we get up and learn from אברהם?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges רב ספרא's method. He does not think we can learn a rule from the way אברהם acted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם lived before מתן תורה, so his conduct may not count as a source for הלכה. רב יוסף's question is rhetorical, and it challenges the basis of רב ספרא's statement.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we arise and learn (derive a rule)

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Shall we arise and derive halakha from Abraham?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source used in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's use of אברהם's conduct as a source for הלכה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The conduct of someone who lived before מתן תורה is not a valid basis for deriving הלכה.

steps.title: רבא: a תנא already learned from אברהם
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רב יוסף's objection by pointing out that a תנא already derived הלכה from אברהם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A תנא learned from אברהם, and we won't learn from him?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back against רב יוסף with a rhetorical question of his own. The next step brings his proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a תנא, who has greater authority than the אמוראים, was willing to learn a rule from אברהם, then surely we may as well. That knocks down רב יוסף's objection in principle.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא, a sage of the משנה period

phrases.english: Rava said:
A tanna derived halakha from Abraham,
and we will not derive from him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנָא גָּמַר מֵאַבְרָהָם וַאֲנַן לָא גָּמְרִינַן מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the קשיא of step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב יוסף's claim that אברהם's conduct cannot serve as a source.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A תנא already relied on אברהם's conduct, so the principle רב יוסף assumes is wrong.

steps.title: Proof from the time of מילה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that מילה may be done all day, but the זריזין do it early, learning this from אברהם rising early for the עקידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.' This teaches that the whole day is valid for מילה. But the זריזין are early to do מצוות, as it says: 'And אברהם rose early in the morning and saddled his donkey.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings the ברייתא that proves his point. The תנא learns the principle of doing מצוות early from אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says only 'the eighth day', so מילה is valid at any hour of that day. The ברייתא adds that eager people do it in the morning, and its source is אברהם getting up early to do the עקידה. This shows a תנא learning practical behavior from אברהם, which supports רב ספרא's statement.

keyTerms.meaning: The whole day is valid for circumcision
The eager are early to do מצוות
And אברהם rose early in the morning

steps.whatToRemember: רבא shows that a תנא did learn practical conduct from אברהם (זריזין מקדימין למצוות). So the objection 'we cannot learn from אברהם' cannot be what bothered רב יוסף. The next step gives רבא's new explanation of רב יוסף's real difficulty.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule זריזין מקדימין למצוות is a basic principle in הלכה. It is why מילה, and many other מצוות, are done early in the day.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not say that doing מילה later in the day is invalid. The whole day is valid. Doing it early is just the preferred way.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
"And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised";
this teaches that the entire day is valid for circumcision,
but the eager are early to perform מצוות,
as it is said:
"And Abraham rose early in the morning and saddled, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: וּבַיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי יִמּוֹל בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source for רבא's claim in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That a תנא derived הלכה from אברהם's conduct
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on מילה, which derives זריזין מקדימין למצוות from 'וישכם אברהם בבקר'

steps.title: רבא restates רב יוסף's real difficulty from the ערב פסח תמיד
steps.stepSummary: רבא says רב יוסף's real problem was a משנה. On ערב פסח that falls on ערב שבת, the תמיד is slaughtered at 6½ hours, not as soon as the walls darken.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: This is what bothered רב יוסף. We learned in a משנה: when ערב פסח falls on ערב שבת, the תמיד is slaughtered at six and a half hours and offered at seven and a half. But then let it be slaughtered as soon as the walls get shadows!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא replaces the earlier understanding of רב יוסף's objection with a new one. The new objection is based on a משנה about when the afternoon תמיד is slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this ערב פסח everyone wants the תמיד as early as possible, so that all the קרבנות פסח can be done before שבת. If מנחה time really starts when shadows appear on the walls (just after 6 hours), it should be slaughtered then. Since the משנה says 6½ hours, it seems we do not follow רב ספרא's 'shadow' rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The day before פסח, when the קרבן פסח is brought
Six and a half hours into the day
The walls darken, meaning shadows appear on them after midday

steps.confusionAlert: The word אלא here does not mean רבא disagrees with the הלכה. It means: 'Rather, רב יוסף's question was really about something else.' The objection from step 5 is being reframed, not dropped.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: רַב יוֹסֵף הָא קָא קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Rav Yosef, this is what was difficult for him.
As we learned in a mishna:

phrases.aramaic: חָל עַרְבֵי פְּסָחִים לִהְיוֹת בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת,
phrases.english: When Pesach eve falls on Shabbat eve,
it (the Tamid) is slaughtered at six and a half hours,
phrases.notes: The afternoon תמיד is moved earlier so the קרבנות פסח can follow it.

phrases.english: and offered on the altar at seven and a half hours.
So let us slaughter it from when the walls darken!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: רַב יוֹסֵף הָא קָא קַשְׁיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reframes רב יוסף's objection (step 5) after רבא showed in steps 6-7 that we do learn הלכה from אברהם.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's rule that מנחה time begins when shadows appear on the walls.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה picks 6½ hours even when the earliest possible time is needed. That suggests מנחה does not start the moment the walls darken.

steps.title: Temple walls only showed shadows at six and a half hours
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the walls of the בית המקדש were built in a way that made them show shadows only at 6½ hours.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difficulty? Maybe the walls of the בית המקדש only darken at six and a half hours, because they are not perfectly straight.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the question with a first answer. In the בית המקדש itself, the walls simply did not show shadows until 6½ hours.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule stays the same: start when the walls darken. The walls of the בית המקדש were wider at the bottom and narrower at the top, so the shadow appeared later. The משנה's 6½ hours therefore fits the 'shadow' rule perfectly.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difficulty? (a formula that opens a rejection)
They are not perfectly straight or aligned

phrases.english: What is the difficulty?
Perhaps the walls of the Temple
darken only at six and a half hours,
because they are not perfectly straight.
phrases.notes: The walls sloped inward toward the top, so the shadow came later.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קוּשְׁיָא? וְדִילְמָא כּוּתְלֵי דְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly rejects the challenge in step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully removes the contradiction between the משנה and the 'shadow' rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question assumed all walls darken right after 6 hours. The walls of the בית המקדש did not.

steps.title: אברהם was different because he knew astronomy
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: אברהם was a great astronomer and could tell the exact moment after midday. Ordinary people need until 6½ hours to be sure.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or alternatively: אברהם was different, because he had great knowledge of astronomy in his heart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different way to reject the question. אברהם had special knowledge that others lack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the real start of מנחה is just after 6 hours, but only an expert can tell that moment for sure. אברהם could, so he davened right away. Everyone else waits until 6½ hours to be certain, and that is why the משנה says 6½.

keyTerms.meaning: Astronomy, knowledge of the movements of the heavens

phrases.english: Or alternatively, Abraham is different,
because great astronomical knowledge was in his heart.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי, שָׁאנֵי אַבְרָהָם דְּאִיצְטַגְנִינוּת גְּדוֹלָה הָיְתָה בְּלִבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Explains the gap between אברהם's time and the משנה's time.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question assumed everyone can detect the moment after midday as precisely as אברהם could.

steps.title: אברהם was different because he was a זקן in ישיבה
steps.stepSummary: Third answer: אברהם was a זקן who sat in ישיבה, so he had the expertise to know the exact time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or alternatively: because he was an elder who sat in a ישיבה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer. אברהם's Torah greatness and his ישיבה gave him precise knowledge of the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works like the second answer: the exact time can only be known by someone with special wisdom. Here the wisdom comes from Torah learning in ישיבה, not from astronomy. The next line brings a source showing that our ancestors always had a ישיבה.

keyTerms.meaning: An elder, a wise Torah scholar
Sits and learns in a ישיבה

phrases.english: Or alternatively, because he was an elder
and sat in a yeshiva.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי, מִשּׁוּם דְּזָקֵן וְיוֹשֵׁב בִּישִׁיבָה הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Explains why אברהם could daven earlier than the time set in the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question ignored אברהם's unique expertise as a זקן in ישיבה.
steps.whatToRemember: All three answers keep the 'shadow' rule and explain the משנה's 6½ hours. Answer 1 says the walls of the בית המקדש darkened late. Answers 2 and 3 say אברהם alone could identify the exact moment.

steps.title: Our ancestors always had a ישיבה
steps.stepSummary: רבי חמא ברבי חנינא teaches that from the days of our ancestors, a ישיבה never left them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי חמא ברבי חנינא said: From the days of our ancestors, a ישיבה never left them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a statement to back up the claim that אברהם sat in ישיבה. This statement then opens a list of proofs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule is stated first: in every era, our ancestors had a ישיבה. The next steps prove it period by period with verses.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Hama, son of Rabbi Hanina, said:
From the days of our ancestors,
a yeshiva never left them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the third answer (step 11) and opens a list of aggadic proofs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Our ancestors always had a Torah ישיבה among them.

steps.title: ישיבה in מצרים and in the מדבר
steps.stepSummary: Verses about gathering the זקני ישראל prove there was a ישיבה in מצרים and in the מדבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: In מצרים there was a ישיבה with them, as it says: 'Go and gather the elders of Israel.' In the מדבר there was a ישיבה with them, as it says: 'Gather for Me seventy men from the elders of Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins proving רבי חמא's statement, starting with the periods of מצרים and the מדבר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'elders' (זקנים) is read as meaning Torah scholars. If there were elders, there was a ישיבה.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a verse)

phrases.english: When they were in Egypt, a yeshiva was with them,
as it says: 'Go and gather the elders of Israel.'
When they were in the desert, a yeshiva was with them,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אֶסְפָה לִּי שִׁבְעִים אִישׁ מִזִּקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״.
phrases.english: as it says: 'Gather for Me seventy men from the elders of Israel.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves רבי חמא's statement for מצרים and the מדבר.
steps.raayaObject: That a ישיבה existed in מצרים and the מדבר.

steps.title: Each of the אבות was a זקן in ישיבה
steps.stepSummary: Verses calling אברהם, יצחק, and יעקב 'old' show that each was a זקן sitting in ישיבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אברהם אבינו was an elder who sat in ישיבה, as it says: 'And אברהם was old, advanced in years.' יצחק אבינו was an elder who sat in ישיבה, as it says: 'When יצחק was old.' יעקב אבינו was an elder who sat in ישיבה, as it says: 'And Israel's eyes were heavy with age.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the proofs, showing that each of the אבות was a זקן in ישיבה. This is the claim that matters for answer 3 about אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אברהם, the verse says both 'old' and 'advanced in years', which seems repetitive. So 'old' (זקן) is read as 'wise elder' and 'advanced in years' as physical age. The same meaning of זקן is applied to יצחק and יעקב.

phrases.english: Abraham our forefather was an elder sitting in yeshiva,
as it says: 'And Abraham was old, advanced in years.'

phrases.aramaic: יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ, זָקֵן וְיוֹשֵׁב בִּישִׁיבָה הָיָה,
phrases.english: Isaac our forefather was an elder sitting in yeshiva,
as it says: 'And it was when Isaac was old.'

phrases.aramaic: יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ, זָקֵן וְיוֹשֵׁב בִּישִׁיבָה הָיָה,
phrases.english: Jacob our forefather was an elder sitting in yeshiva,
as it says: 'And Israel's eyes were heavy with age.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of proofs, now covering the אבות.
steps.raayaObject: That אברהם, יצחק, and יעקב were each a זקן in ישיבה.

steps.title: אליעזר mastered his master's Torah
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר עבד אברהם is called 'the elder of his house who ruled over all he had'. רבי אלעזר explains that he had mastery of his master's Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליעזר, servant of אברהם, was an elder who sat in ישיבה, as it says: 'And אברהם said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had.' רבי אלעזר said: He ruled over (mastered) the Torah of his master.
steps.whatsHappening: The list extends even to אברהם's servant, אליעזר, who was also a Torah scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Ruled over all he had' is read by רבי אלעזר as being about Torah. אליעזר had mastered all of אברהם's Torah. This shows how deeply ישיבה learning ran in אברהם's household.

keyTerms.meaning: Had mastery of his teacher's Torah

phrases.english: Eliezer, servant of Abraham,
was an elder sitting in yeshiva,
as it says: 'And Abraham said to his servant,

phrases.aramaic: זְקַן בֵּיתוֹ הַמֹּשֵׁל בְּכׇל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ״,
phrases.english: the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had,'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: שֶׁמּוֹשֵׁל בְּתוֹרַת רַבּוֹ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said: That he had mastery over his master's Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֱלִיעֶזֶר עֶבֶד אַבְרָהָם, זָקֵן וְיוֹשֵׁב בִּישִׁיבָה הָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the list of proofs to אליעזר.
steps.raayaObject: That אליעזר was a זקן in ישיבה who mastered אברהם's Torah.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית כד:ב, with רבי אלעזר's reading

steps.title: דמשק means he drew and gave others to drink
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads 'דמשק אליעזר' as a word play: he drew (דולה) and gave others to drink (משקה) from his master's Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He is דמשק אליעזר'. רבי אלעזר said: He would draw and give others to drink from his master's Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second teaching from רבי אלעזר. אליעזר did not only master אברהם's Torah; he also taught it to others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דמשק is read as a blend of דולה ('draws') and משקה ('gives to drink'). Torah is pictured as water. אליעזר drew it from אברהם and passed it on. This finishes the picture of a living ישיבה in אברהם's house.

keyTerms.meaning: Damascus, read as a word play on דולה ומשקה
Draws water and gives others to drink

steps.whatToRemember: This is the end of the section. The 'shadow' rule for מנחה survives. The משנה's 6½ hours is explained by the late shadows on the walls of the בית המקדש, or by אברהם's unique expertise from astronomy or from his ישיבה. The aggadic list shows that Torah ישיבה was always part of our ancestors' lives.

phrases.english: 'He is Damascus Eliezer' —
Rabbi Elazar said:
That he draws and gives to drink
from his master's Torah to others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second verse and reading about אליעזר that builds on step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That אליעזר taught אברהם's Torah to others.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית טו:ב, with רבי אלעזר's word play

steps.title: אברהם kept the entire Torah
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that אברהם אבינו kept the whole Torah, based on the פסוק 'עקב אשר שמע אברהם בקולי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: אברהם אבינו kept the entire Torah, as it says: 'Because Abraham listened to My voice, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: Building on the idea that the אבות learned Torah, רב adds a new claim: אברהם actually kept the whole Torah, long before it was given at סיני.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof comes from בראשית כ״ו:ה, which goes on to say that אברהם kept 'My charge, My מצוות, My laws and My Torahs.' Because the פסוק lists so many kinds of commandments, רב reads it as covering the entire Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: the entire Torah, all of it

phrases.english: Rav said:
Abraham our father fulfilled
the entire Torah, all of it,
as it is said: 'Because ... listened'
phrases.notes: This פסוק is from בראשית כ״ו:ה.

phrases.english: Abraham to My voice, etc.'
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points to the rest of the פסוק: 'My charge, My מצוות, My laws, and My Torahs'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: קִיֵּים אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Related to the previous steps about the אבות and Torah learning; it moves from learning Torah to keeping all of it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אברהם אבינו kept the whole Torah, as shown by the פסוק 'עקב אשר שמע אברהם בקולי'.

steps.title: Maybe אברהם kept only the seven מצוות of בני נח
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר חייא suggests the פסוק might only mean the seven מצוות of בני נח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר חייא said to רב: But say it means only the seven מצוות!
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר חייא pushes back on רב by offering a smaller reading of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every human being is commanded in the seven מצוות of בני נח. So perhaps the praise for אברהם is only that he kept those seven. If so, the פסוק would not prove that he kept the whole Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: but say instead (a suggested alternative reading)
the seven מצוות given to all of mankind (בני נח)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שִׁימִי בַּר חִיָּיא לְרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya said to Rav:
But say: the seven מצוות?
phrases.notes: These are the seven מצוות given to all of Noah's descendants.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how broadly רב reads the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's reading that the פסוק means the entire Torah
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק could just as easily mean the seven מצוות of בני נח, so it does not prove the whole Torah.

steps.title: But אברהם also kept מילה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the 'seven מצוות' reading, because אברהם clearly also kept מילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is also circumcision!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a problem with the 'only seven מצוות' suggestion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מילה is not one of the seven מצוות of בני נח, yet the Torah clearly says אברהם did it. So he certainly kept more than just the seven.

phrases.english: But there is also circumcision!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the פסוק refers only to the seven מצוות
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: אברהם definitely kept מילה, which goes beyond the seven מצוות.

steps.title: Then say seven מצוות plus circumcision
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is adjusted: perhaps אברהם kept the seven מצוות plus מילה, and nothing more.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then say: the seven מצוות and circumcision!
steps.whatsHappening: The challenger fixes the suggestion by adding מילה, but still argues against the claim of the whole Torah.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding מילה answers the problem raised in step 19. The challenge remains: there is still no proof that אברהם kept the entire Torah.

phrases.english: Then say: the seven מצוות and circumcision!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Revises the objection of step 18 after the rejection in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that אברהם kept the whole Torah
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eight מצוות (the seven plus מילה) explain everything we know, so the whole Torah is not proven.

steps.title: The extra words 'My מצוות and My Torahs' prove more
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that if only eight מצוות were meant, the פסוק would not need the words 'מצותי ותורותי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: If so, why do I need 'My מצוות and My Torahs'?
steps.whatsHappening: רב defends his position by pointing to the extra words in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses broad, plural terms: 'My מצוות' and 'My Torahs.' Those words would be unnecessary if it meant only eight specific מצוות. They show that אברהם kept the full range of the Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: why do I need it? (the word seems extra)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, the broad, plural wording of the פסוק shows that אברהם kept the entire Torah, not just the seven מצוות of בני נח plus מילה.

phrases.english: He (Rav) said to him:
If so, 'My מצוות and My Torahs'
why do I need?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן מִצְוֹתַי וְתוֹרוֹתָי לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording in the פסוק (a word would otherwise be unnecessary)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק might refer only to eight מצוות.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words 'מצותי ותורותי' cover the entire Torah.

steps.title: אברהם kept even the rabbinic עירובי תבשילין
steps.stepSummary: רב (or רב אשי) says אברהם kept even עירובי תבשילין, because the plural 'תורותי' includes the Oral Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said, and some say רב אשי: אברהם אבינו kept even עירובי תבשילין, as it says 'My Torahs': one is the Written Torah and one is the Oral Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement goes even further: אברהם kept rabbinic laws too, such as עירובי תבשילין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'תורותי' is plural, so it refers to two Torahs: the תורה שבכתב and the תורה שבעל פה. Keeping the Oral Torah includes even small rabbinic details like עירובי תבשילין, which was instituted much later.

keyTerms.meaning: a rabbinic setup of cooked food that allows cooking on יום טוב for שבת

steps.confusionAlert: עירובי תבשילין is a rabbinic enactment that did not yet exist in אברהם's time. The point is that אברהם kept the Torah in such detail that he observed even this.

phrases.english: Rav said, and some say Rav Ashi:
Abraham our father fulfilled
even the joining of cooked foods,
as it is said: 'My Torahs' (plural),
one, the Written Torah,
and one, the Oral Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: קִיֵּים אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ אֲפִילּוּ עֵירוּבֵי תַבְשִׁילִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רב's statement from step 17 to include rabbinic law.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אברהם kept both the Written and the Oral Torah, even עירובי תבשילין.

steps.title: Who says 'Yes' in מתיא בן שמואל's version?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה of מתיא בן שמואל and asks who answers 'הן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: מתיא בן שמואל says, etc. ... and he says 'Yes.' Who says 'Yes'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה about checking for dawn and sets up a question: which person answers 'הן'? This question prepares the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the ממונה asks: 'Is the whole eastern sky lit, even until חברון?' Then the משנה says 'he says Yes.' The משנה does not make clear who 'he' is, so the גמרא asks.

phrases.english: Matya ben Shmuel says, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' points back to the משנה: 'Is the whole eastern sky lit, even until Hebron?'

phrases.english: and he says: Yes.
Who said 'Yes'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadic side discussion and returns to the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which person in the משנה answers 'הן': the one on the roof or the one on the ground?

steps.title: The man on the roof cannot both ask and answer
steps.stepSummary: If the one on the roof says 'הן', then he is answering his own question, which makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is the one standing on the roof, does he dream and also interpret?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first option and finds a problem with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person on the roof is the one who can see the sky. If he also answers 'yes', then he is answering his own question, like someone who dreams a dream and then interprets it himself. That would make the question pointless.

phrases.english: If you say it is that one standing on the roof —
does he dream and he interpret?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to the question of step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The option that the man on the roof says 'הן'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One person cannot both ask the question and answer it.

steps.title: The man on the ground cannot know
steps.stepSummary: If the one on the ground says 'הן', how would he know? He cannot see the sky from there.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is the one standing on the ground. But how does he know?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the second option and finds a problem with it too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person on the ground cannot see far enough to tell whether the light has reached חברון. So he has no way to answer 'yes.' Both options now seem impossible.

phrases.english: Rather, it is that one standing on the ground,
from where does he know?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָךְ דְּקָאֵי אַאַרְעָא מְנָא יָדַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the second option after the first was rejected in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The option that the man on the ground says 'הן'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He cannot see the sky, so he has no knowledge to answer with.

steps.title: It could be either person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that either person could be the one who says 'הן', and promises to explain each option.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you wish, say it is the one on the ground; and if you wish, say it is the one on the roof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two possible answers and sets up an explanation of each one in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each option can work if we picture the conversation differently. The גמרא now has to explain how each version avoids the problem raised against it.

keyTerms.meaning: if you wish, say (introduces one of two possible answers)

phrases.english: If you wish, say — that one standing on the ground,
and if you wish, say — that one standing on the roof.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא הָךְ דְּקָאֵי אַאַרְעָא וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא הָךְ דְּקָאֵי אַאִיגָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two problems raised in steps 24 and 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two possible ways of reconstructing the conversation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Neither person could be the one who says 'הן'.
steps.terutzMaskana: Either one could be, depending on how the conversation went.

steps.title: How the man on the roof can say Yes
steps.stepSummary: The man on the roof announces that the east is lit, the man on the ground asks 'until חברון?', and the man on the roof answers 'הן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you wish, say it is the one on the roof: he says, 'The whole east is lit!' The one on the ground asks him, 'Until חברון?' And he answers, 'Yes!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first option: the conversation goes in an order where the man on the roof answers someone else's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man on the roof is not answering himself. He first makes a general announcement, then the man on the ground asks a follow-up question, and the man on the roof answers it. This avoids the 'dreams and interprets' problem from step 24.

keyTerms.meaning: the whole face of the east is lit

phrases.english: If you wish, say it is that one standing on the roof,
he said: 'The face of the entire east is lit!'
and that one standing on the ground said to him:
'Even until Hebron?'
and he said to him: 'Yes!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא הָךְ דְּקָאֵי אַאִיגָּרָא אָמַר אִיהוּ הֵאִיר פְּנֵי כׇּל הַמִּזְרָח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the roof option from step 26 and resolves the problem of step 24.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The man on the roof would be answering his own question.
steps.terutzMaskana: The man on the roof answers the ground man's follow-up question, so he is not asking and answering himself.

steps.title: Second option: the man on the ground says 'הן'
steps.stepSummary: Alternatively, the man on the ground asks if the whole east is lit, the man on the roof asks 'until חברון?', and the man on the ground confirms 'הן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say it is the man standing on the ground. He asks, 'Is the whole eastern sky lit?' The man on the roof asks back, 'Do you mean all the way to חברון?' The man on the ground answers, 'Yes!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second way to read the משנה, as it promised in step 26. This time the person on the ground is the one who says 'הן'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 asked how the man on the ground could say 'הן' when he cannot see the sky. Here the answer is that he is not reporting what he sees. He is only confirming what he meant by his own question. The man on the roof is the one checking the sky.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another possible answer
Hebron, the city where the light must reach

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'הן' does not mean 'I see the light reaching חברון.' It means 'Yes, that is what I was asking about.' That is why the man on the ground can say it.
steps.whatToRemember: Either man can say 'הן'. Whoever says it is answering the other man's follow-up question about חברון, so he never answers his own question and never claims to see what he cannot.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say
the one who is standing on the ground:
he says, 'Is the whole eastern sky lit?'
And the man on the roof says to him, 'Until Hebron?'
phrases.notes: The man on the roof is asking what the man on the ground meant.

phrases.english: And the man on the ground says to him, 'Yes!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second option, after step 27 gave the first.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different reading of who says each line
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The man on the ground could not say 'הן' because he cannot see the sky.
steps.terutzMaskana: He says 'הן' only to confirm what his own question meant.

steps.title: Can moonlight really be mistaken for sunrise?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's question about why the careful check was needed, then challenges the story behind it: can moonlight and sunlight really be confused?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה asked: 'Why did they need this check?' (The answer there was that once they mistook moonlight for sunrise.) The גמרא asks: Can those two lights really be confused?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה and questions the incident it describes. This sets up a source that will back the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the dawn check was made because people once brought the תמיד too early, thinking moonlight was sunrise. The גמרא doubts that such a mistake is realistic. If the two lights look clearly different, the story seems hard to accept.

keyTerms.meaning: And are they really confused with each other?
Etc.: the rest of the quoted text continues

phrases.english: 'And why did they need this?' etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, whose answer was that moonlight was once mistaken for sunrise.

phrases.english: But are they really confused?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of the announcement to the reason the משנה gives for it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's story that moonlight was mistaken for sunrise
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the two lights look clearly different, the mistake should not have happened.

steps.title: A ברייתא: moonlight and sunlight look different
steps.stepSummary: רבי teaches that moonlight rises in a straight column like a stick, while sunlight spreads out in all directions.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a ברייתא teaches that רבי says: A column of moonlight is not like a column of sunlight. Moonlight rises straight up like a stick. Sunlight spreads out to this side and that side.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support its challenge. The ברייתא shows that the two lights look different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי gives a clear visual difference. Moonlight is a narrow beam, while sunrise spreads wide. That makes the משנה's story even harder to understand.

keyTerms.meaning: A column or pillar of light
Like a stick, meaning straight and narrow
Spreads out to here and there

phrases.english: But it was taught: Rabbi says:
A column of moonlight is not similar
to a column of sunlight.

phrases.aramaic: תִּימּוּר שֶׁל לְבָנָה מִתַּמֵּר וְעוֹלֶה כְּמַקֵּל,
phrases.english: A column of moonlight rises straight up like a stick;

phrases.aramaic: תִּימּוּר שֶׁל חַמָּה מַפְצִיעַ לְכָאן וּלְכָאן.
phrases.english: a column of sunlight spreads out to here and to there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind the challenge in step 29.
steps.raayaObject: That moonlight and sunlight cannot easily be confused
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in the name of רבי

steps.title: It was a cloudy day
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל teaches that it was cloudy, so the moonlight also spread out and looked like sunrise.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: It was a cloudy day, and the moonlight spread out to this side and that side.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The mistake happened on a cloudy day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally moonlight is a narrow beam, as רבי said. Clouds scatter it so that it spreads wide like sunrise. רבי's rule is correct for a clear sky, and the משנה's mistake happened in unusual weather.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in the school of רבי ישמעאל

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
It was a cloudy day,
and the moonlight spread out to here and to there.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל: יוֹם הַמְעוּנָּן הָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 29 and 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Special circumstance that changes how things look
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Moonlight always looks like a narrow stick, so no one could mistake it for sunrise.
steps.terutzMaskana: Clouds made the moonlight spread out, so it looked like sunrise.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי's rule describes a clear sky. Clouds scatter moonlight and make it spread like sunrise, and that is how the mistake in the משנה happened.

steps.title: רב פפא: a cloudy day counts as fully sunny
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא learns from this that on a cloudy day, sunlight is spread everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Learn from this that a cloudy day is entirely sun.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא draws a new rule from the cloudy-day answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clouds spread moonlight everywhere, so they must spread sunlight everywhere too. On a cloudy day, the sun's effect reaches every place, not only where the sun shines directly.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: Learn from this:
a cloudy day is entirely sun.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general rule from the answer in step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a cloudy day, sunlight is spread everywhere.

steps.title: What practical difference does this make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical result comes from רב פפא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What practical difference does this make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב פפא's rule matters in practice. This sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to know where it would matter that a cloudy day counts as sunny everywhere.

phrases.english: For what is there a practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical use of step 32.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where רב פפא's rule makes a difference

steps.title: First difference: spreading hides to dry
steps.stepSummary: On a cloudy day, hides can be spread to dry anywhere, because the sun reaches everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: For spreading hides to dry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first practical example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone drying leather does not need to find a spot in direct sunlight on a cloudy day. Every outdoor spot gets the sun's effect.

keyTerms.meaning: To spread out hides to dry

phrases.english: For spreading hides.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Hides dry anywhere outside on a cloudy day.

steps.title: Second difference: kneading מצה
steps.stepSummary: Following רבא, a woman may not knead מצה dough in the sun or with sun-heated water, so on a cloudy day she may not knead it anywhere outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else, it matters for what רבא taught: A woman may not knead dough in the sun, and not with water heated by the sun.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second practical example, this one from the laws of מצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heat from the sun can make the dough become חמץ. רבא forbids kneading in the sun. Because a cloudy day counts as sunny everywhere, she may not knead anywhere outdoors on such a day.

phrases.english: Alternatively, for what Rava taught:
A woman may not knead in the sun
and not with water heated by the sun.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the question of step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No kneading of מצה anywhere outside on a cloudy day.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רב פפא's observation about light has a real halachic result for baking מצה.

steps.title: רב נחמן: hazy sunlight is harsher than direct sun
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says hazy sunlight through clouds is harsher than plain sunlight, with a jar of vinegar as a memory aid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The haze of the sun is harder than the sun itself. Your memory aid is a jar of vinegar.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the topic is cloudy days, the גמרא brings a related saying of רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sunlight held back by clouds comes out stronger, like the smell of vinegar from a sealed jar when it is opened. The memory aid helps you remember the idea.

keyTerms.meaning: The haze of the sun, sunlight through clouds

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
The haze of the sun is harsher than the sun,
and your memory aid: a jar of vinegar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related teaching about cloudy-day sunlight.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hazy sunlight is harsher than direct sunlight.

steps.title: רב נחמן: broken sunlight is harsher than full sun
steps.stepSummary: Sunlight breaking through gaps in the clouds is harsher than full sunlight, with dripping water as a memory aid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bright flashes of sun through the clouds are harder than the sun itself. Your memory aid is a drip.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן continues with a second, similar saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Light that bursts through cracks in the clouds bothers the eyes more than steady sunlight. In the same way, water dripping on a person bothers him more than being fully in water.

keyTerms.meaning: Broken, dazzling sun rays through gaps in clouds

phrases.english: Broken rays of the sun are harsher than the sun,
and your memory aid: a drip.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second saying of רב נחמן on the same theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Broken sun rays are harsher than full sunlight.
steps.whatToRemember: Clouds do not weaken the sun's effect. Light through clouds spreads everywhere (רב פפא), and hazy or broken sunlight can be even harsher than direct sun (רב נחמן).
